name: Vamanapureeswarar Temple, Tirumanikuzhi
deity: Shiva as Vamanapureeswarar (Vamaneeswarar), with the goddess Ambujakshi
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine sung in the Tevaram (7th century); with later Chola additions and inscriptions
summary: Vamanapureeswarar at Tirumanikuzhi is an old Shiva temple of the Cuddalore country, praised by Sambandar in the Tevaram and tied in its legends to Vishnu's Vamana avatara and the humbling of the king Mahabali.

sections.history: Tirumanikuzhi lies in the Cuddalore country of the old Nadu Nadu, and its temple has been a place of Shaiva worship since the age of the Nayanars, for Sambandar sang of Vamanapureeswarar in the Tevaram and made it a Paadal Petra Sthalam. The shrine is old in its foundations, and the later Cholas left their mark upon it: inscriptions from the reigns of Rajaraja the Great and Kulothunga record gifts and works here. Kept in worship across the centuries, it remains a quiet village temple with a long memory.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east beneath a five-tiered gopuram, and its shrines are gathered within three concentric courts enclosed by granite walls. The sanctum holds the linga of Vamanapureeswarar, while the goddess Ambujakshi is honoured in her own shrine, which faces north. The old stone of the enclosures carries the inscriptions of the Chola kings, and the unhurried plan of courts and mandapas is in the manner of the temples of this region.
sections.legends: The legends of Tirumanikuzhi reach back to Vishnu's Vamana avatara and the king Mahabali. One story tells of a lamp in the temple whose wick was tugged by a rat, and that the creature, for the merit of having stirred the sacred flame, was reborn as the generous king Mahabali; and it was before Mahabali that Vishnu came as the dwarf Vamana, measured the worlds in three strides, and set his foot upon the humbled king to grant him grace. The Sun too is said to have worshipped Shiva here. In these tales the temple binds the Shaiva shrine to the great story of the dwarf and the king.
sections.festivals: The Purattasi Navarathri in September or October is kept with devotion, and Maha Shivaratri in February or March is the great night of the year, with worship through its watches. The monthly Pradosham is observed as at every Shiva temple. Dates follow the Tamil calendar, so confirm them locally, especially for festival days.
sections.experience: Tirumanikuzhi is a village temple that rewards a quiet visit. Enter beneath the eastern gopuram, pass through the granite courts to the sanctum of Vamanapureeswarar, and come to the north-facing shrine of the goddess Ambujakshi. Those who know the story of Vamana and Mahabali will find it close at hand here, and the old inscriptions on the walls reward an unhurried eye. The temple suits a traveller passing through the Cuddalore country who likes a shrine with a long memory.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Tirumanikuzhi lies in Cuddalore district, near Panruti on the Cuddalore road; Cuddalore and Villupuram are the nearest railheads, and Puducherry the nearest airport. Buses serve the village from Cuddalore and Panruti, and the temple stands at its centre.
